evals.prompt: We run a hotel booking SaaS product. We're considering adding a Go library that's licensed under AGPL-3.0 to handle PDF invoice generation on our backend, which customers reach only over the network (we never distribute the binary to them). Is this safe to add without legal review?
evals.expected_output: Flags AGPL as triggering source-release obligations even for network-only SaaS use (no distribution required), and recommends escalating to legal before adding it.

assertions.text: Identifies AGPL's network-use trigger, not just distribution
Recommends legal review/escalation rather than approving unilaterally

evals.prompt: A teammate wants to statically link an LGPL-licensed C library into our proprietary Go binary that we ship to customers as a single compiled executable. They say 'LGPL is fine to use in proprietary software, so this is no problem.' Evaluate this reasoning.
evals.expected_output: Explains that LGPL's weak-copyleft exception typically relies on the library being dynamically linked/swappable, and that static linking into a single binary is a more contested case that needs closer scrutiny, not an automatic pass.

assertions.text: Flags static linking as different from dynamic linking under LGPL
Does not simply approve the plan as unconditionally fine

evals.prompt: We want to add a small Apache-2.0 licensed Go utility library (no transitive dependencies) to our proprietary backend service that we never distribute in source form. Is this safe to add, and why?
evals.expected_output: Confirms Apache-2.0 is permissive and safe to use in proprietary software without triggering source-release obligations, noting its explicit patent grant as a bonus.

assertions.text: Identifies Apache-2.0 as permissive/safe for proprietary use
Does not incorrectly demand legal escalation for a routine permissive license

not_contains: requires legal sign-off before any use
